question.text: A trader holds an equity portfolio and writes cash-settled index calls against it. If the market rallies sharply above the call strike, what is the net outcome?

answer.text: The portfolio gains value but net upside is capped — gains on the portfolio above the strike are offset by losses on the short index calls (cash-settled), so the writer keeps the premium plus appreciation up to the strike but gives up gains beyond it
The portfolio loses value and the call expires worthless, giving the writer a net loss
The covered call writer earns unlimited profit since they hold the underlying
Both the portfolio and the written call generate profits simultaneously

explanation.text: The Logic: A covered-call style structure here is long equity portfolio + short index call. Above the strike, the short call's cash-settled payoff is negative (settlement − strike, paid out by the writer), and this offsets the portfolio's mark-to-market gains above the strike. Net upside ≈ appreciation up to the strike + premium received. The Trap: The writer does NOT have unlimited profit — the short call caps the net upside. Above the strike, the written call's losses move inversely to portfolio gains, not in the same direction. Note: Strictly, the textbook covered call is written against the specific stock held, with delivery / cash-settlement matching the share position. With cash-settled index calls written against a diversified portfolio, the offset is by mark-to-market cash flow on the index option rather than by delivery of the equity portfolio, so basis between portfolio and index can leave residual P&L.
